Then when the imam comes out, the scrolls are folded up, the pens are lifted, and the angels gather at the pulpit listening to the remembrance»}. And it is said that people, in their proximity when gazing upon the face of God—exalted is He—are in proportion to their earliness in going to Friday.

Then, when you enter the mosque, seek the first row. When the people have gathered, do not step over their necks, nor pass before them while they are praying. Sit near a wall or a pillar so that no one passes before you. And do not sit until you have prayed the greeting of the mosque (taḥiyyah); the better practice is to pray four cycles (rakʿāt), reciting in each cycle after the Opening (al-Fātiḥah) the Sincerity (al-Ikhlāṣ) fifty times. For in the report: {«Whoever does that will not die until he sees his seat in Paradise, or it is shown to him»}. And do not abandon the greeting even if the imam is delivering the sermon.

It is recommended on this day, or in its night, to pray four cycles with four chapters: Sūrat al-Anʿām, al-Kahf, Ṭā Hā, and Yā Sīn. If you cannot manage that, then Sūrat Yā Sīn and al-Dukhān, and Alif-Lām-Mīm al-Sajdah, and Sūrat al-Mulk. And do not neglect reciting these chapters on Friday night, for in them is abundant merit. Whoever cannot do that well, let him increase in reciting Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ. And send abundant blessings upon the Messenger of God—peace and blessings be upon him—on this day especially.

Whenever the imam comes out, cut off prayer and speech, and occupy yourself with responding to the caller to prayer (muʾadhdhin), then with listening to the sermon and taking admonition from it. And abandon speech altogether during the sermon. For in the report: {«Whoever says to his companion—while the imam is delivering the sermon—"Listen!" or "Be quiet!" has spoken vainly; and whoever speaks vainly has no Friday»}—that is, because his saying "Listen!" is speech. Thus one should admonish others by gesture, not by utterance.

Then follow the imam as previously mentioned. When you finish and give the greeting of peace (salām), recite the Opening (al-Fātiḥah) seven times before speaking, the Sincerity (al-Ikhlāṣ) seven times, and the two refuge-seeking chapters (al-Muʿawwidhatān) seven times each. That will protect you until the next Friday and be a safeguard for you against Satan. Then say after that: "O Self-Sufficient (Yā Ghanī), O Praiseworthy (Yā Ḥamīd), O Originator (Yā Mubdiʾ), O Restorer (Yā Muʿīd), O Merciful (Yā Raḥīm), O Loving (Yā Wadūd); enrich me with Your lawful provision (ḥalāl) from Your forbidden (ḥarām), and with Your obedience from Your disobedience, and with Your bounty from all besides You." Then pray after Friday two cycles, or four, or six, in pairs—all of that is transmitted from the Messenger of God—peace and blessings be upon him—in different circumstances.

Then remain in the mosque until sunset (maghrib) or until the afternoon prayer (ʿaṣr), and be excellent in watching for the noble hour; for it is indeterminate throughout the entire day. Perhaps you may attain it while you are humble before God—exalted is He—submissive and supplicating.

And do not attend in the mosque the circles of storytelling (majālis al-qaṣaṣ), but rather the circle of beneficial knowledge—that which increases your fear of God—exalted is He—and diminishes your desire for this world. For every knowledge that does not call you from this world to the Hereafter, ignorance of it is more beneficial to you than it. So seek refuge with God from knowledge that does not profit.

And multiply supplication at sunrise, at the sun's zenith (zawāl), at sunset, at the commencement of the prayer (iqāmah), at the ascension of the preacher to the pulpit, and at the standing of the people for prayer—perhaps the noble hour may fall within some of these times.

And strive to give charity on this day with whatever you can, even if little, so that you combine prayer, fasting, charity, recitation, remembrance, seclusion (iʿtikāf), and vigilance (ribāṭ).

And make this day of the week especially for your Hereafter; perhaps it may be an expiation for the rest of the week.

chapters.title_en: The Etiquette of Fasting and the Second Section: On Avoiding Sins
chapters.arabic_text:
### | آداب الصيام

لا ينبغي أن تقتصر على صوم رمضان فتترك التجارة بالنوافل، وكسب الدرجات
العالية في الفراديس؛ فتتحسر إذ نظرت إلى منازل الصائمين، كما تنظر إلى
الكواكب  الدرية، وهم في أعلى عليين.
والأيام الفاضلة التي شهدت الأخبار بشرفها وفضلها، وبجزالة الثواب في
صيامها: يوم عرفة لغير الحاج، ويوم عاشوراء، والعشر الاول من ذي الحجة،
والعشر الأول من المحرم، ورجب وشعبان، وصوم الأشهر الحرم من الفضائل، وهي
ذو القعدة وذو الحجة والمحرم ورجب، واحد فرد وثلاثة سرد، وهذه في السنة.
وأما في الشهر فأول الشهر وأوسطه وآخره، والأيام البيض وهي الثالث عشر
والرابع عشر والخامس عشر، وأما في الاسبوع فيوم الاثنين والخميس والجمعة؛
فتكفر ذنوب الاسبوع بصوم الاثنين والخميس والجمعة، وتكفر ذنوب الشهر باليوم
الأول واليوم الأوسط واليوم الآخر والأيام البيض، وتكفر ذنوب السنة بصيام
هذه الأيام والاشهر المذكورة.
ولا تظن إذا صمت أن الصوم هو ترك الطعام والشراب والوقاع فقط، فقد قال
صلى الله عليه وسلم: (كم من صائم ليس له من صيامه إلا الجوع والعطش) ، بل
تمام الصوم بكف الجوارح كلها عما يكرهه الله تعالى، بل ينبغي أن تحفظ العين
عن النظر إلى المكاره، واللسان عن النطق بما لا يعنيك، والأذن عن الاستماع
إلى ما حرمه الله؛ فإن المستمع شريك
القائل وهو أحد المغتابين، وكذلك تكف جميع الجوارح كما تكف البطن والفرج،
ففي الخبر (خمس يفطرن الصائم: الكذب، والغيبة، والنميمة، واليمين الكاذبة،
والنظر بشهوة) ، وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: (إنما الصوم جنة فإذا كان أحدكم
صائما فلا يرفث، ولا يفسق، ولا يجهل، فإن امرؤ قاتله أو شاتمه فليقل: إني
صائم) .
ثم اجتهد أن تفطر على طعام حلال، ولا تستكثر فتزيد على ما تأكله كل ليلة،
فلا فرق إذا استوفيت ما تعتاد أن تأكله دفعتين في دفعة واحدة، وإنما
المقصود بالصيام كسر شهوتك، وتضعيف قوتك لتقوى بها على التقوى. فإذا أكلت
عشية ما تداركت به ما فتك ضحوة، فلا فائدة في صومك، وقد ثقلت عليك معدتك،
وما وعاء يملأ أبغض إلى الله تعالى من حلال، فكيف إذا ملىء من حرام؟
فإذا عرفت معنى الصوم فاستكثر منه ما استطعت، فإنه أساس العبادات، ومفتاح
القربات؛ قال رسول الله صلى  الله عليه وسلم: (قال الله تعالى: كل حسنة بعشر
أمثالها إلى سبعمائة ضعف إلا الصوم، فإنه لي وأنا أجزى به) ، وقال صلى الله
عليه وسلم: (والذي نفسي بيده لخلوف فم الصائم أطيب عند الله من ريح المسك،
يقول الله تعالى عزوجل من قائل: إنما يذر شهوته وطعامه وشرابه من أجلى،
فالصوم لي وأنا أجزى به) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: (للجنة باب له الريان،
لا يدخله إلا الصائمون) .
فهذا القدر من شرح الطاعات يكفيك من بداية الهداية، فإذا احتجت إلى
الزكاة، والحج، أو إلى مزيد شرح الصلاة والصيام، فاطلبه مما أوردناه في
كتابنا (إحياء علوم الدين) .

### | القسم الثاني

القول في اجتناب المعاصى

### | توطئة

اعلم ان للدين شطرين، أحدهما: ترك المناهي، والآخر: فعل الطاعات.. وترك
المناهي هو الأشد؛ فإن الطاعات يقدر عليها كل واحد، وترك الشهوات لا يقدر
عليه إلا الصديقون،
فلذلك قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: (المهاجر من هجر السوء،
والمجاهد من جاهد هواه) .
واعلم أنك إنما تعصي الله بجوارحك، وهي نعمة من الله عليك وأمانة لديك،
فاستعانتك بنعمة الله على معصيته غاية الكفران، وخيانتك في أمانة استودعها
الله غاية الطغيان؛ فأعضاؤك رعاياك، فانظر كيف ترعاها؛ فكلكم راع، وكلكم
مسؤول عن رعيته.
واعلم أن جميع أعضائك ستشهد عليك في عرصات القيامة بلسان طلق ذلق، تفضحك
به على رؤوس الخلائق، قال الله تعالى: (يوم تشهد عليهم ألسنتهم وأيديهم
وأرجلهم بما كانوا يعملون) ، وقال الله تعالى: (اليوم نختم على افواههم
وتكلمنا أيديهم وتشهد أرجلهم بما كانوا يكسبون) . فاحفظ يا مسكين جميع بدنك
من المعاصى، وخصوصا أعضاءك السبعة؛ فإن جهنم لها سبعة أبواب لكل باب منهم
جزء مقسوم، ولا يتعين لتلك الابواب إلا من عصا الله تعالى بهذه الاعضاء
السبعة، وهي: العين، والأذن، واللسان، والبطن، والفرج، واليد، والرجل.

### | آداب العين

أما العين: فإنما خلقت لك لتهتدي بها في الظلمات، وتستعين بها في
الحاجات، وتنظر بها إلى عجائب ملكوت الأرض والسموات، وتعتبر بما فيها من
الآيات؛ ن فاحفظها عن أربع: أن تنظر  بها إلى غير محرم، أو إلى صورة مليحة
ولا بشهوة نفس، أو تنظر بها إلى مسلم بعين الاحتقار، أو تطلع بها على عيب
مسلم.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ص-و-م (ṣ-w-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "abstention" (imsāk) from food, drink, and speech; lexically, it denotes refraining from any act.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Sharīʿah, it is the specific abstention from appetites (shahawāt) with the intention of drawing near to God; its essence is the veiling of the soul from worldly allurements.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the ritual fast; metaphorically (majāz) for the silence of the tongue and the restraint of all limbs from sin.
- Root: ه-ج-ر (h-j-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To abandon, forsake, or emigrate; the root implies severing ties with a place or a habit.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The "emigrant" (muhājir) in the prophetic saying is one who abandons what God has forbidden—an internal hijrah from sin.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical migration; metaphorical for the soul's flight from disobedience to obedience.
- Root: ج-ن-ن (j-n-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cover, conceal, or shield; the "jannah" (paradise) is so named for its covering of trees; "jinn" are hidden from sight.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The fast as a "shield" (junnah) signifies a protective covering against the Fire, both in this world and the next.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a physical shield; metaphorical for the fast's protective function against sin and punishment.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — In the phrase "If a man fights him or reviles him, let him say: 'I am fasting,'" the protasis (sharṭ) and apodosis (jawāb) are governed by the imperative (amr), indicating a binding command that the fasting person must respond with restraint, not retaliation.
chapters.translation:
### | The Etiquette of Fasting

You should not confine yourself to the fast of Ramadan, thereby abandoning the trade of supererogatory fasts and the acquisition of lofty stations in the highest paradises; for you will then be filled with regret when you gaze upon the abodes of those who fast, just as you gaze upon the brilliant stars, while they are in the most exalted heights (ʿilliyyīn).

The virtuous days whose excellence and merit, and whose abundant reward for fasting, have been attested by the reports (akhbār) are: the Day of ʿArafah for one who is not a pilgrim, the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, the first ten days of Muḥarram, Rajab and Shaʿbān. And fasting the sacred months (al-ashhur al-ḥurum) is among the virtues—these being Dhū al-Qaʿdah, Dhū al-Ḥijjah, Muḥarram, and Rajab: one being solitary and three consecutive. These are within the year.

As for within the month: the beginning of the month, its middle, and its end, and the white days (al-ayyām al-bīḍ)—namely the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth. As for within the week: Monday, Thursday, and Friday. Thus, the sins of the week are expiated by fasting Monday, Thursday, and Friday; the sins of the month are expiated by the first day, the middle day, the last day, and the white days; and the sins of the year are expiated by fasting these aforementioned days and months.

Do not suppose that when you fast, the fast is merely the abandonment of food, drink, and sexual intercourse alone. For he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "How many a faster has nothing from his fast but hunger and thirst." Rather, the completion of the fast lies in restraining all the limbs from what God Almighty dislikes. Indeed, you must guard the eye from looking at what is detestable, the tongue from uttering what does not concern you, and the ear from listening to what God has forbidden; for the listener is a partner of the speaker, being one of the backbiters. Likewise, restrain all the limbs just as you restrain the belly and the private parts. For in the report: "Five things break the fast of the faster: lying, backbiting, slander, false oath, and looking with lust." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Verily, the fast is a shield; so when one of you is fasting, let him not utter obscenity, nor act wickedly, nor behave ignorantly. And if a man fights him or reviles him, let him say: 'I am fasting.'"

Then strive to break your fast with lawful (ḥalāl) food, and do not eat excessively so as to exceed what you normally eat each night. For there is no difference if you consume in one sitting what you are accustomed to eating in two sittings. The sole purpose of the fast is to break your appetite and weaken your strength so that you may thereby be empowered for piety (taqwā). If you eat in the evening what you make up for what you missed in the forenoon, then there is no benefit in your fast, and your stomach has become heavy upon you. And no vessel that a human fills is more detestable to God Almighty than a lawful one—so how then if it is filled with the unlawful?

When you have understood the meaning of the fast, then multiply it as much as you are able, for it is the foundation of acts of worship and the key to acts of nearness. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "God Almighty said: 'Every good deed is rewarded tenfold up to seven hundredfold, except the fast, for it is Mine, and I shall reward it.'" And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "By Him in Whose hand is my soul, the bad breath of the faster's mouth is more fragrant to God than the scent of musk. God Almighty says: 'He only abandons his appetite, his food, and his drink for My sake. So the fast is for Me, and I shall reward it.'" And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Paradise has a gate called al-Rayyān; none shall enter it except the fasters."

This measure of explanation of acts of obedience suffices you from The Beginning of Guidance. If you have need of the alms-tax (zakāh), the pilgrimage (ḥajj), or a more detailed explanation of the prayer and the fast, then seek it from what we have set forth in our book, The Revival of the Religious Sciences (Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn).

### | The Second Section

The Discourse on Avoiding Sins

### | Introduction

Know that religion has two halves: one is the abandonment of prohibitions, and the other is the performance of acts of obedience. And the abandonment of prohibitions is the more severe; for acts of obedience are within the capacity of everyone, whereas the abandonment of appetites is within the capacity of none but the veracious (ṣiddīqūn). For this reason, the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The emigrant is one who emigrates from evil, and the striver is one who strives against his own desire."

Know that you only disobey God with your limbs, and they are a blessing from God upon you and a trust (amānah) in your keeping. Your using God's blessing to disobey Him is the utmost ingratitude, and your betrayal of the trust that God has deposited with you is the utmost transgression. Your limbs are your subjects; so consider how you shepherd them. For each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock.

Know that all your limbs will bear witness against you in the plains of the Resurrection with an eloquent, fluent tongue, exposing you before the heads of creation. God Almighty said: {«On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet bear witness against them as to what they used to do»} (Q 24:24). And God Almighty said: {«Today We seal their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness as to what they used to earn»} (Q 36:65). So guard, O wretched one, your entire body from sins, especially your seven limbs; for Hell has seven gates, and for each gate there is an apportioned share. And none are assigned to those gates except those who disobey God Almighty with these seven limbs—namely: the eye, the ear, the tongue, the belly, the private parts, the hand, and the foot.

### | The Etiquette of the Eye

As for the eye: it was only created for you to guide yourself by it in darkness, to aid yourself with it in your needs, to behold by it the wonders of the dominion (malakūt) of the earth and the heavens, and to take heed of the signs contained therein. So guard it from four things: that you look with it at what is unlawful, or at a comely form with lust of the soul, or that you look at a Muslim with an eye of contempt, or that you pry with it into the fault of a Muslim.

chapters.title_en: The Etiquette of the Ear and the Tongue, and the Eight Vices of the Tongue — Section 15
chapters.arabic_text:
### | آداب الأذن

وأما الأذن: فاحفظها عن أن تصغي بها إلى البدعة، أو الغيبة، أو الفحش،
أالخوض في الباطل، أو ذكر مساوىء الناس؛ فإنما خلقت لك لتسمع بها كلام الله
تعالى، وسنة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، وحكمة أوليائه، وتتوصل باستفادة
العلم بها إلى الملك المقيم والنعيم الدائم في جوار رب العالمين. فإذا
أصغيت بها إلى شيء من المكاره صار ما كان لك عليك، وانقلب ما كان سبب فوزك
سبب هلاكك، وهذا غية الخسران. ولا تظن أن الإصم يختص به القائل دون
المستمع؛ ففي الخبر: (أن المستمع شريك القائل وهو أحد المغتابين) .
آداب اللسان وأما اللسان: فإنما خلق لتكثر به ذكر الله تعالى وتلاوة
كتابه، وترشدن به خلق الله تعالى إلى طريقه، وتظهر به ما في ضميرك من حاجات
دينك ودنياك. فإذا استعملته في غير ما خلق له، فقد كفرت نعمة
الله تعالى فيه، وهو أغلب أعضائك عليك وعلى سائر الخلق، ولا يكب الناس في
النار على مناخرهم إلا حصائد ألسنتهم.
فاستظهر عليه بغاية قوتك حتى لا يكبك في قعر جهنم، ففي الخبر: (إن الرجل
ليتكلم بالكلمة ليضحك بها أصحابه فيهوي بها في قعر جهنم سبعين خريفا) ،
وروى أنه قتل شهيد في المعركة على عهد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال
قائل: ن هنيئا له الجنة، فقال: صلى الله عليه وسلم: (وما يدريك لعله كان
يتكلم فيما لا يعنيه، ويبخل بما لا يغنيه) .
فاحفظ لسانك من ثمانية:

### | الأول الكذب

فاحفظ منه لسانك في الجد والهزل، ولا تعود لسانك الكذب هزلا فيتداعى إلى
الجد، والكذب من أمهات الكبائر، ثم إنك إذا عرفت بذلك سقطت عدالتك والثقة
بقولك، وتزدريك الأعين وتحتقرك.
وإذا أردت أن تعرف قبح الكذب من نفسك، فانظر إلى كذب غيرك، وعلى نفرة
نفسك عنه، واستحقارك لصاحبه واستقباحك له.
وكذلك فافعل في جميع عيوب نفسك؛  فإنك لا ترى قبح عيوبك من نفسك، بل من
غيرك، فما استقبحته من غيرك يستقبحه غيرك منك لا محلاة؛ فلا ترض لنفسك ذلك.

### | الثاني الخلف في الوعد

فإياك أن تعد بشيء ولا تفي به، بل ينبغي أن يكون إحسانك إلى الناس فعلا
بلا قول، فإن اضطررت إلى الوعد، فإياك أن تخلف إلا لعجز أو ضرورة؛ فإن ذلك
من امارات النفاثق وخبائث الاخلاق، قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: (ثلاث من
كن فيه فهو منافق وإن صام وصلى: من إذا حدث كذب، وإذا وعد أخلف، وإذا أؤتمن
خان) .

### | الثالث الغيبة

فاحفظ لسانك عنها، والغيبة أشد من ثلاثين زنية في الاسلام. كذلك ورد في
الخبر.
ومعنى الغيبة: أن تذكر إنسانا بما يكرهه لو سمعه، فأنت مغتاب ظالم وإن
كنت صادقا.
وإياك وغيبة القراء المرائين، وهو أن تفهم المقصود من غير تصريح فتقول:
أصلحه الله فقد ساءني وغمني ما جرى عليه، فنسأل الله تعالى أن يصلحنا
وإياه؛ فإن هذا جمع بين خبيثين، أحدهما: الغيبة إذا حصل به التفهم، والآخر:
تزكية النفس والثناء عليها بالتجريح
لغيرك والصلاح لنفسك. ولكن إن كان مقصودك من قولك: أصلحه الله - الدعاء؛
فادع له في السر. وإن اغتممت بسببه، فعلامة أنك لا تريد فضيحته واظهار
عيبه، وفي إظهارك الغم بعيبه إظهار تعييبه.
ويكفيك زاجرا عن الغيبة قوله تعالى: (ولا يغتب بعضكم بعضا، أيحب أحدكم أن
يأكل لحم أخيه ميتا فكرهتموه) . فقد شبهك الله بآكل لحم الميتة؛ فما أجدرك
أن تحترز منها؟؟؟! ويمنعك عن الغيبة أمر لو تفكرت فيه وهو أن تنظر في نفسك،
هل فيك عيب ظاهر أو باطن؟، وهل أنت مقارف معصية سرا أو جهرا؟ فإذا عرفت ذلك
من نفسك، فاعلم أن عجزه عن التنزهي عما نسبته إليه كعجزك، وعذره كعذرك.
وكما تكره أن تفتضح وتذكر عيوبك، فهو أيضا يكرهه؛ فإن سترته ستر الله عليك
عيوبك، وإن فضحته سلط الله عليك ألسنة حدادا، يمزقون عرضك في الدينا، ثم
يفضك الله في الآخرة على رؤوس الخلائق يوم القيامة.
وإن  نظرت إلى ظاهرك وباطنك، فلم تطلع فيهما على عيب ونقص في دين ولا
دنيا، فاعلم أن جهلك بعيوب نفسك أقبح أنواع الحماقة، ولا عيب أعظم من
الحمق. ولو أراد الله بك خيرا لبصرك بعيوب نفسك، فرؤيتك نفسك بعين الرضا
غاية غباوتك وجهلك. ثم إن كنت صادقا في ظنك فاشكر الله تعالى عليه ولا
تفسده بثلب الناس، والتمضمض بأعراضهم؛ فإن ذلك من أعظم العيوب.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-ذ-ن (ʾ-dh-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The ear as the organ of hearing; derived from the notion of perceiving and heeding (iṣghāʾ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Hearing as the gateway to divine discourse (kalām Allāh) and prophetic tradition; the ear is a trust (amānah) from God.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal hearing (samʿ) versus figurative heedfulness (iṣghāʾ); the ear's purpose is teleological — created for guidance, not for vice.
- Root: ل-س-ن (l-s-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The tongue as the instrument of speech; root denotes articulation and expression of the inner self (ḍamīr).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The tongue is a divine blessing (niʿmah) for dhikr and guidance; its misuse constitutes ingratitude (kufrān al-niʿmah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal organ versus metaphorical "tongue" as the faculty of utterance; the ḥaṣāʾid (harvests) of the tongue are its spoken deeds.
- Root: غ-ي-ب (gh-y-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Absence or concealment; ghībah as mentioning another in a way they would dislike.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Backbiting as a moral violation of the unseen (ghayb) — attacking what is hidden about a person; equated with consuming carrion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal absence versus metaphorical consumption of flesh; the Quranic simile is a rhetorical taṣwīr (vivid depiction) of moral repugnance.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — In "المستمع شريك القائل وهو أحد المغتابين", the pronoun "هو" resumes the subject for explicative emphasis, binding the listener's sin to the speaker's, as parsed in the ḥadīth's conditional structure.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the servant's limbs are each a trust from God, and upon each is an obligation of propriety. Now, as for the ear: guard it from inclining toward innovation (bidʿah), backbiting (ghībah), obscenity, plunging into falsehood, or mentioning the faults of people. For it was created for you only that you might hear thereby the speech of God Most High, the Sunnah of His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), and the wisdom of His saints, and that through acquiring knowledge you might attain to the abiding kingdom and the everlasting bliss in the vicinity of the Lord of the Worlds. So if you incline it toward any of these detested things, that which was for you becomes against you, and that which was the cause of your success becomes the cause of your destruction — and this is the utmost loss. Do not suppose that the sin of listening is confined to the speaker alone, excluding the hearer; for in the report: «The listener is a partner of the speaker, and he is one of the backbiters.»

As for the tongue: it was created only that you might multiply thereby the remembrance of God Most High and the recitation of His Book, that you might guide God's creatures to His path, and that you might express thereby what is in your conscience of the needs of your religion and your worldly life. So if you employ it for other than that for which it was created, you have been ungrateful for God's blessing therein — and it is the most dominant of your limbs over you and over all creatures. Nothing casts people into the Fire upon their nostrils save the harvests of their tongues. So seek aid against it with all your might, lest it cast you into the depths of Hell; for in the report: «A man indeed speaks a word to make his companions laugh, and thereby he plummets into the depths of Hell for seventy autumns.» And it is related that a man was killed as a martyr in battle during the era of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), and a speaker said: "How blessed for him is Paradise!" He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «What makes you know? Perhaps he used to speak about what did not concern him, and withhold what did not avail him.»

So guard your tongue from eight things:

### The First: Lying (Kadhib)
Guard your tongue from it in seriousness and in jest. Do not accustom your tongue to lying in jest, lest it slide into seriousness. Lying is among the gravest of the major sins (kabāʾir). Moreover, if you become known for it, your moral probity (ʿadālah) falls and trust in your word is lost; eyes disdain you and hold you in contempt. If you wish to recognize the ugliness of lying from yourself, then look at the lying of others — at your own soul's aversion to it, your contempt for its practitioner, and your deeming it foul. Do likewise regarding all your own faults; for you do not see the ugliness of your own faults from yourself, but rather from others. Whatever you deem ugly in another, another deems ugly in you — without doubt. So do not consent to that for yourself.

### The Second: Breaking Promises (Khalaf al-Waʿd)
Beware of promising something and then not fulfilling it. Rather, your beneficence to people should be action without speech. If you are compelled to promise, then beware of breaking it except due to incapacity or necessity; for that is among the signs of hypocrisy and the vilest of character traits. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «Three qualities — whoever possesses them is a hypocrite, even if he fasts and prays: one who, when he speaks, lies; when he promises, breaks it; and when he is entrusted, betrays.»

### The Third: Backbiting (Ghībah)
Guard your tongue from it. Backbiting is more severe than thirty acts of fornication in Islam — thus it is reported in the tradition. The meaning of backbiting is: that you mention a person with something he would dislike if he heard it. So you are a backbiter and a wrongdoer, even if you are truthful. Beware especially of the backbiting of ostentatious reciters (qurrāʾ murāʾīn) — which is that you convey the intended meaning without explicit statement, saying: "May God set him right; what befell him has pained and grieved me; we ask God to set us and him aright." For this combines two vile things: one is backbiting, if comprehension is thereby achieved; the other is self-justification and self-praise — by disparaging another while claiming righteousness for oneself. But if your intention in saying "May God set him right" is supplication (duʿāʾ), then supplicate for him in secret. And if you are grieved on his account, that is a sign that you do not intend his exposure or the display of his fault — whereas your displaying grief over his fault is itself a display of fault-finding against him. Sufficient as a deterrent from backbiting is His saying Most High: {«And do not backbite one another; would any of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would abhor it»} (Q. 49:12). He has likened you to an eater of carrion — how fitting that you should beware of it! And what prevents you from backbiting is a matter, if you reflected upon it: that you look into yourself — is there in you an apparent or hidden fault? Are you committing a sin secretly or openly? If you know that of yourself, then know that his inability to be free of what you attributed to him is like your inability, and his excuse is like your excuse. Just as you hate to be exposed and to have your faults mentioned, so too does he hate it. If you conceal him, God conceals your faults; if you expose him, God unleashes upon you sharp tongues that tear apart your honor in this world, then God exposes you in the Hereafter before the heads of all creatures on the Day of Resurrection. And if you examine your outward and inward state and find in them no fault or deficiency in religion or worldly matters, then know that your ignorance of your own faults is the ugliest kind of foolishness — and no fault is greater than foolishness. Had God willed good for you, He would have shown you your own faults; your seeing yourself with an eye of self-satisfaction is the extreme of your dullness and ignorance. Then, if you are truthful in your assumption, thank God Most High for it, and do not corrupt it by defaming people and rinsing your mouth with their honors; for that is among the greatest of faults.

chapters.title_en: The Fourth Vice: Disputation, Quarreling, and Arguing with People in Speech
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الرابع المراء والجدال ومناقشة الناس في الكلام

فذلك فيه إيذاء للمخاطب وتجهيل له، وطعن فيه، وفيه ثناء على النفس وتزكية
لها بمزيد الفطنة والعلم، ثم هو مشوش للعيش؛ فإنك لا تمارى سفيها إلا
ويؤذيك، ولا تماري حليما إلا ويقليك ويحقد عليك؛ فقد قال صلى الله عليه
وسلم: (من ترك المراء وهو مبطل بنى الله له بيتا في ربض الجنة، ومن ترك
المراء وهو محق بنى الله له بيتا في أعلى الجنة) .
ولا ينبغي أن يخدعك الشيطان ويقول لك: أظهر الحق ولا تداهن فيه، فإن
الشيطان أدبا يستجر الحمقى إلى الشر في معرض الخير، فلا تكن ضحكة للشيطان
فيسخر منك، فاظهار الحق حسن مع من يقبله منك، وذلك بطريق النصيحة في الخفية
لا بطريق المماراة.
وللنصيحة صفة وهيئة، ويحتاج
فيها إلى تلطف وإلا صارت فضيحة، وكان فسادها أكثر من صلاحها.
ومن خالط متفقهة العصر غلب على طبعه المراء والجدال، وعسر عليه الصمت، إذ
ألقى إليه علماء السوء أن ذلك هو الفضل، والقدرة على المحاجة والمناقشة هو
الذي يمتدح به؛ ففر منهم فرارك من الأسد، واعلم أن المراء سبب المقت
عندالله وعند الخلق.

### | الخامس تزكية النفس

فقد قال الله تعالى: (فلا تزكوا أنفسكم هو أعلم بمن اتقى) ، وقيل بعض
الحكماء: مالصدق القبيح؟ فقال: ثناء المرء على نفسه. فإياك أن تتعود ذلك،
واعلم أن ذلك ينقص من قدرك عند الناس، ويوجب مقتك عندالله تعالى. فإذا أردت
أن تعرف أن ثناءك على نفسك لا يزيد في قدرك عند غيرك، فانظر إلى أقرانك إذا
أثنوا على أنفسهم بالفضل والجاه والمال كيف يستنكره  قلبك عليهم، ويستثقله
طبعك، وكيف تذمهم عليه إذا فارقتهم؛ فاعلم أنهم أيضا في حال تزكيتك لنفسك
يذمونك في قلوبهم ناجزا، وسيظهرونه بألسنتهم إذا فارقتهم.
السادس: اللعن
فإياك أن تلعن شيئا مما خلق الله تعالى من حيوان أو طعام أو إنسان بعينه،
ولا تقطع بشهادتك على أحد من أهل القبلة بشرك أو كفر أو نفاق؛ فإن المطلع
على السرائر هو الله تعالى، فلا تدخل بين العباد وبين الله تعالى، واعلم
أنك يوم القيامة لا يقال لك: لم لم تلعن فلانا، ولم سكت عنه؟ بل لو لم تعلن
ابليس طول عمرك، ولم تشغل لسانك بذكره لم تسأل عنه ولم تطالب به يوم
القيامة. وإذا لعنت أحدا من خلق الله تعالى طولبت به، ولا تذم شيئا مما خلق
الله تعالى، فقد كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يذم الطعام الردىء قط، بل
كان إذا اشتهى شيئا أكله وإلا تركه.

### | السابع الدعاء على الخلق

فاحفظ لسانك عن الدعاء على أحد من خلق الله تعالى، وإن ظلمك فكل أمره إلى
الله تعالى؛ ففي الحديث: (إن المظلوم ليدعو على ظالمه حتى يكافئه ثم يبقى
للظالم فضل عنده يطالب به يوم القيامة) . وطول بعض الناس لسانه على الحجاج
فقال بعض السلف: (إن الله لينتقم للحجاج ممن تعرض له بلسانه كما ينتقم من
الحجاج لمن ظلمه) .

### | الثامن المزاح والسخرية والاستهزاء بالناس

فاحفظ
لسانك منه، في الجد والهزل؛ فإنه يريق ماء الوجه ويسقط المهابة، ويستجر
الوحشية، ويؤذي القلوب، وهو مبدأ اللجاج والغضب والتصارم، ويغرس الحقد في
القلوب؛ فلا تمازح أحدا؛ فإن مازحك أحد فلا تجبه، وأعرض عنهم حتى يخوضوا في
حديث غيره، وكن من الذين إذا مروا باللغو مروا كراما.
فهذه مجامع آفات اللسان، ولا يعينك عليه إلا العزلة، أو ملازمة الصمت غلا
بقدر الضرورة؛ فقر كان أبوبكر الصديق رضي الله تعالى عنه يضع حجرا في فيه
ليمنعه ذلك من الكلام بغير ضرورة، ويشير إلى لسانه ويقول: هذا الذي أوردني
الموارد. فاحترز منه بجهدك؛ فإنه أقوى أسباب هلاكك  في الدنيا والآخرة.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: م ر ي (m-r-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To dispute, to contend, to wrangle; the root carries the sense of milking a she-camel (drawing out milk with effort), implying the strained extraction of arguments.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Disputation (mirāʾ) is blameworthy contention in speech, seeking to expose another's error for dominance, not for truth.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) is the physical drawing forth; metaphorical (majāz) is the contentious extraction of words in debate.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ) — The Prophet's saying uses conditional constructions (man taraka... banā Allāhu) where the protasis (condition) and apodosis (result) are linked by the particle "man," indicating a universal causal relation.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the fourth vice—disputation, quarreling, and arguing with people in speech—there is in this an injury to the one addressed, a declaration of his ignorance, and an aspersion cast upon him. There is also in it self-praise and self-justification through an excess of cleverness and knowledge. Moreover, it disturbs one's livelihood; for you never dispute with a fool but that he harms you, nor do you dispute with a forbearing man but that he detests you and harbors rancor against you. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«مَنْ تَرَكَ الْمِرَاءَ وَهُوَ مُبْطِلٌ بَنَى اللهُ لَهُ بَيْتًا فِي رَبَضِ الْجَنَّةِ، وَمَنْ تَرَكَ الْمِرَاءَ وَهُوَ مُحِقٌّ بَنَى اللهُ لَهُ بَيْتًا فِي أَعْلَى الْجَنَّةِ»} ("Whoever abandons disputation while being in the wrong, Allah builds for him a house in the outskirts of Paradise; and whoever abandons disputation while being in the right, Allah builds for him a house in the highest part of Paradise").

It behooves you not to be deceived by Satan when he says to you: "Proclaim the truth and do not flatter in it." For Satan is an adab-teacher who lures the foolish toward evil under the guise of good. So do not become a laughingstock for Satan, that he may mock you. Indeed, proclaiming the truth is good with one who accepts it from you—but that is by way of sincere counsel (naṣīḥah) in secret, not by way of disputation. Sincere counsel has a quality and a manner; it requires gentleness and delicacy, otherwise it becomes a scandal, and its corruption outweighs its soundness.

Whoever mingles with the jurisprudents of his age has his natural disposition overcome by disputation and quarreling, and silence becomes difficult for him—since the evil scholars have cast into him that this is excellence, and that the ability to argue and debate is what one is praised for. So flee from them as you would flee from a lion. Know that disputation is a cause of divine wrath (maqt) with Allah and with creation.

I say: As for the fifth vice—self-justification (tazkiyat al-nafs)—Allah Most High has said: {«فَلَا تُزَكُّوا أَنْفُسَكُمْ هُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِمَنِ اتَّقَى»} ("So do not justify yourselves; He knows best who fears Him"). It was said to one of the sages: "What is ugly truthfulness?" He replied: "A man's praise of himself." Beware of accustoming yourself to this, and know that it diminishes your standing with people and necessitates divine wrath upon you from Allah Most High. If you wish to know that your self-praise does not increase your standing with others, then look at your peers when they praise themselves for excellence, status, or wealth—how your heart disapproves of it in them, how your nature finds it burdensome, and how you censure them for it when you part from them. Know likewise that they, at the moment of your self-justification, censure you in their hearts immediately, and they will manifest it with their tongues when you part from them.

I say: As for the sixth vice—cursing (laʿn)—beware of cursing anything that Allah Most High has created, whether animal, food, or a specific person. Do not pronounce a verdict by your testimony against any of the people of the qiblah (Muslims) of shirk (polytheism), kufr (disbelief), or nifāq (hypocrisy). For the One who inspects the innermost secrets is Allah Most High. So do not interpose yourself between the servants and Allah Most High. Know that on the Day of Resurrection you will not be asked: "Why did you not curse so-and-so, and why did you remain silent about him?" Rather, even if you had not cursed Iblis your entire life, and had not occupied your tongue with his mention, you would not be questioned about him nor called to account for him on the Day of Resurrection. But if you curse any of Allah's creation, you will be called to account for it. Do not disparage anything that Allah Most High has created, for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) never disparaged bad food at all; rather, if he desired something he ate it, and if not, he left it.

I say: As for the seventh vice—supplication against creation (duʿāʾ ʿalā al-khalq)—guard your tongue from supplicating against anyone of Allah's creation, even if he wrongs you; for his entire affair is referred to Allah Most High. In the hadith: {«إِنَّ الْمَظْلُومَ لَيَدْعُو عَلَى ظَالِمِهِ حَتَّى يُكَافِئَهُ ثُمَّ يَبْقَى لِلظَّالِمِ فَضْلٌ عِنْدَهُ يُطَالَبُ بِهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ»} ("Indeed, the wronged one supplicates against his wrongdoer until he is recompensed, then there remains a surplus for the wrongdoer with him, which he will be called to account for on the Day of Resurrection"). Some people lengthened their tongues against al-Ḥajjāj, and one of the Salaf said: "Indeed, Allah takes vengeance for al-Ḥajjāj against whoever assails him with his tongue, just as He takes vengeance from al-Ḥajjāj for those he wronged."

I say: As for the eighth vice—jesting, mockery, and derision of people—guard your tongue from it, in both seriousness and jest. For it causes the water of the face to flow away, topples dignity, draws forth wildness, injures hearts, and is the beginning of stubbornness, anger, and estrangement. It plants rancor in hearts. So do not jest with anyone; and if someone jests with you, do not respond to him. Turn away from them until they engage in other discourse, and be among those who, when they pass by vain talk, pass by with dignity. {«وَالَّذِينَ إِذَا مَرُّوا بِاللَّغْوِ مَرُّوا كِرَامًا»} ("And those who, when they pass by vain talk, pass by with dignity").

These are the comprehensive categories of the afflictions of the tongue. Nothing aids you against them except seclusion (ʿuzlah) or adhering to silence except to the measure of necessity. It is said that Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah Most High be pleased with him) used to place a stone in his mouth to prevent himself from speaking without necessity, and he would point to his tongue and say: "This is what has brought me to the watering-places of ruin." So be on your guard against it with all your effort, for it is the strongest of the causes of your destruction in this world and the Hereafter.

chapters.title_en: The Etiquette of the Stomach, the Private Parts, and the Hands
chapters.arabic_text:
### | آداب البطن

وأما البطن: فاحفظه من تناول الحرام والشبهة، واحرص على طلب الحلال، فإذا
وجدته فاحرص على أن تقتصر منه على ما دون الشبع، فإن الشبع يقسي القلب،
ويفسد الذهن، ويبطل الحفظ، ويثقل الأعضاء عن العبادة والعلم، ويقوي
الشهوات، وينصر جنود الشيطان.
والشبع من الحلال مبدأ كل شر، فكيف من الحرام وطلب الحلال فريضة على كل
مسلم، والعبادة مع أكل الحرام كالبناء على السرجين.
فإذا قنعت في السنة بقميص خشن، وفي اليوم والليلة برغيفين من الخشكار،
وتركت التلذذ بأطيب الأدم، لم يعوزك من الحلال ما يكفيك، والحلال كثير.
وليس بعليك أن تتيقن بواطن الأمور، بل عليك أن تحترز مما تعلم أنه حرام
أو تظن أنه حرام ظنا حصل من علامة ناجزة مقدرة بالمال؛ أما المعلوم فظاهر،
وأما المظنون بعلامة فهو مال السلطان وعماله، ومال من لا كسب له إلا من
النياحة، أو بيع الخمر، أو الربا، أو المزامير؛ وغير ذلك من آلات اللهو
المحرمة. فإن من علمت أن أكثر ماله حرام قطعا، فما تأخذه من يده - وإن أمكن
ان يكون حلالا نادرا - فهو حرام؛ لأنه الغالب على الظن.
ومن الحرام المحض ما يؤكل من الأوقاف من غير شرط الواقف، فمن لم يشتغل
بالتفقه فما يأخذه من المدارس حرام، ومن ارتكب معصية ترد بها شهادته، فما
يأخذه باسم الصوفية من وقف أو غيره فهو حرام.
وقد ذكرنا مداخل الشبهات والحلال والحرام في كتاب مفرد من كتب إحياء علوم
الدين، فعليك بطلبه؛ فإن معرفة الحلال وطلبه فريضة على كل مسلم، كالصلوات
الخمس.

### | آداب الفرج

وأما الفرج: فاحفظه عن كل ما حرم الله تعالى، وكن كما قال الله: (والذين
هم لفروجهم حافظون، إلا على أزواجهم أو ما
ملكت أيمانهم غير ملومين) .
ولا تصل إلى حفظ الفرج إلا بحفظ العين عن النظر، وحفظ القلب عن التفكر،
وحفظ البطن عن الشبهة وعن الشبع؛ فإن هذه محركات للشهوة ومغارسها.

### | آداب اليدين

وأما اليدان: فاحفظهما عن أن تضرب بهما مسلما، أو تتناول بهما مالا
حراما، أو تؤدي بهما أحدا من الخلق، أو تخون بهما في أمانة أو وديعة، أو
تكتب بهما ما لا يجوز النطق به، فإن القلم أحد اللسانين، فاحفظ القلم عما
يجب حفظ اللسان عنه.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش ب ع (sh-b-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Satiety, fullness of the belly; the opposite of hunger (jūʿ). Its core sense is repletion that quenches desire entirely.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the theological register, shabaʿ denotes a physical state that dulls the heart's receptivity to divine remembrance (dhikr) and weighs down the limbs from obedience (ṭāʿah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for bodily repletion; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to the heart—"satiated with heedlessness" (shabʿān min al-ghaflah)—signaling spiritual torpor.
- Root: ح ر م (ḥ-r-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be forbidden, sacred, inviolable; the root carries a dual sense of prohibition and sanctity, as in al-ḥaram (the sacred precinct).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥarām is that which the Law (Sharʿ) has decisively interdicted, whether in substance (ʿayn) or acquisition (kasb); its opposite is ḥalāl.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for what is legally prohibited; metaphorical in "ḥarīm al-dār" (the protected precinct of a house), extending to the inviolable bounds of God's commands.
- Root: ش ب ه (sh-b-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Resemblance, ambiguity; that which is unclear due to similarity between the permissible and the forbidden.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Shubhah (pl. shubuhāt) is the middle ground where evidence for licitness and prohibition is balanced; the pious abstain from it as a shield for religion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for visual resemblance; metaphorical for moral equivocation—"the affair is shrouded in shubhah" (ashbaha al-amr), i.e., its ruling is obscured.
- Root: ف ر ج (f-r-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The private part; also a cleft or opening. Its root sense is "to open, to relieve," hence faraj (relief from distress).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Quranic verse cited, ḥifẓ al-faraj (guarding the private part) is a comprehensive term for chastity (ʿiffah), encompassing the limbs and the heart.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the bodily organ; metaphorical for the "opening" of one's honor—guarding it is guarding one's entire moral integrity.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — In the phrase "فاحفظه من تناول الحرام والشبهة" (guard it from consuming the forbidden and the ambiguous), the conjunction wa (and) coordinates two distinct categories, not synonyms; each retains its independent legal force, requiring separate vigilance.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the stomach, guard it from consuming what is forbidden (ḥarām) and what is ambiguous (shubhah), and strive earnestly in seeking what is lawful (ḥalāl). When you find it, then be diligent to restrict yourself to less than full satiety (shabaʿ), for satiety hardens the heart, corrupts the intellect, nullifies memory, weighs down the limbs from worship and knowledge, strengthens the passions, and reinforces the soldiers of Satan.

Satiety from lawful food is the beginning of every evil—so how then [is it] with what is forbidden? And seeking lawful sustenance is an obligation (farīḍah) upon every Muslim. Worship while consuming the forbidden is like building upon dung.

If you are content in a year with a coarse shirt, and in a day and night with two loaves of coarse barley bread (khushkār), and you abandon delighting in the choicest of condiments, then lawful provision sufficient for you will not be lacking—for lawful things are abundant.

It is not incumbent upon you to ascertain the inner realities of all matters; rather, you must be cautious of what you know to be forbidden, or what you deem forbidden by a presumption (ẓann) arising from a decisive indicator estimable by wealth. As for what is known [to be forbidden], it is manifest. As for what is presumed [forbidden] by an indicator, it is the wealth of the ruler and his officials, and the wealth of one who has no means of earning except through wailing [for the dead], or selling wine, or usury (ribā), or flutes—and other instruments of forbidden amusement. For if you know with certainty that most of one's wealth is forbidden, then whatever you take from his hand—even if it could rarely be lawful—is forbidden, because the predominant presumption (ghalabat al-ẓann) [renders it so].

Among that which is purely forbidden (ḥarām maḥḍ) is what is eaten from endowments (awqāf) contrary to the stipulation of the endower (al-wāqif). Thus, whoever does not occupy himself with jurisprudence (fiqh), whatever he takes from the schools (madāris) is forbidden. And whoever commits a sin that invalidates his legal testimony (shahādah), whatever he takes in the name of Sufism (al-ṣūfiyyah) from an endowment or otherwise is forbidden.

We have already mentioned the entrances of ambiguities (shubuhāt), the lawful, and the forbidden in a separate book among the books of Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn. It is incumbent upon you to seek it, for knowing the lawful and seeking it is an obligation upon every Muslim, like the five daily prayers.

I say: As for the private part (farj), guard it from everything that God—exalted is He—has forbidden, and be as God said: {«وَالَّذِينَ هُمْ لِفُرُوجِهِمْ حَافِظُونَ، إِلَّا عَلَىٰ أَزْوَاجِهِمْ أَوْ مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ فَإِنَّهُمْ غَيْرُ مَلُومِينَ»} (And those who guard their private parts, except from their spouses or what their right hands possess—for indeed they are not blameworthy). You will not attain the guarding of the private part except by guarding the eye from looking, guarding the heart from reflection [upon lustful thoughts], and guarding the stomach from ambiguity and from satiety—for these are the movers of desire and its seedbeds.

I say: As for the two hands, guard them from striking a Muslim with them, from taking forbidden wealth with them, from harming any of creation with them, from betraying with them a trust (amānah) or a deposit (wadīʿah), or from writing with them what is not permissible to utter—for the pen is one of the two tongues. So guard the pen from what the tongue must be guarded from.

chapters.title_en: Section 18 — The Etiquette of the Two Feet and the Sins of the Heart
chapters.arabic_text:
### | آداب الرجلين

وأما الرجلان: فاحفظهما عن أن تمشي بهما إلى حرام، أو تسعى بهما إلى باب
سلطان ظالم؛ فإن المشي إلى السلاطين الظلمة من غر ضرورة وارهاق معصية
كبيرة؛ فإنه تواضع وإكرام لهم على ظلمهم.
وقد أمر الله تعالى بالإعراض عنهم في قوله تعالى: (ولا تركنوا إلى الذين
ظلموا فتمسكم النار) وهو تكثير لسوادهم، وإن ذلك لسبب طلب مالهم فهو سعى
إلى حرام، وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم: (من تواضع لغنى صالح لغناه ذهب ثلثا
دينه) وهذا في غنى صالح، فما ظنك بالغنى الظالم؟ وعلى الجملة، فحركاتك
وسكناتك بأعضائك نعمة من نعم الله تعالى عليك؛ فلا تحرك شيئا منها في معصية
الله تعالى أصلا، واستعملها في طاعة الله تعالى.
واعلم أنك إن قصرت فعليك وباله، وإن شمرت فإليك تعود ثمرته، والله غني
عنك وعن عملك، وإنما كل نفس بما كسبت رهينة، وإياك أن تقول: إن الله كريم
رحيم يغفر الذنوب للعصاة؛ فإن هذه كلمة حق أريد بها باطل، وصاحبها ملقب
بالحماقة، بتلقيب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حيث قال: (الكيس من دان
نفسه وعمل لما بعد الموت، والأحمق من أتبع نفسه هواها، وتمنى على الله
الأماني) . واعلم أن قولك هذا أيضا هي قول من يريد أن يكون فقيها في علوم
الدين من غير أن يدرس علما واشتغل بالبطالة وقال: إن الله كريم رحيم قادر
على أن يفيض على قلبي من العلوم ما أفاضه على قلوب أنبيائه وأوليائه من غير
جهد وتكرار وتعلم وهو كقول من
يريد مالا فترك الحراثة والتجارة والكسب ويتعطل، وقال: إن الله كريم رحيم
وله خزائن السموات والأرض وهو قادر على أن يطلعني على كنز من كنوز أستغني
به عن الكسب، فقد فعل ذلك لبعض عباده، فأنت إذا سمعت كلام هذين الرجلين
استحمقتهما وسخرت منهما، وإن كان ما وصفاه من كرم الله تعالى وقدرته صدقا
وحقا، فكذلك يضحك عليك أرباب البصائر في الدين إذا طلبت المغفرة بغير سعى
لها، والله وتعالى يقول: (وأن ليس للإنسان إلا ما سعى) ، ويقول: (إنما
تجزون ما كنتم تعملون) ويقول (إن الأبرار لفي نعيم، وإن الفجار لفى جحيم) .
فإذا لم تكن تترك السعي في طلب العلم والمال اعتمادا على كرمه، فكذلك لا
تترك التزود للآخرة، ولا تفتر؛ فإن رب الدنيا واللآخرة واحد، وهو فيهما
كريم رحيم، وليس يزيد له كرم بطاعتك وإنما كرمه سبحانه وتعالى في أن ييسر
لك طريق الوصول الى الملك المقيم والنعيم الدائم المخلد، بالصبر على ترك
الشهوات أياما قلائل، وهذا نهاية الكرم.
فلا تحدث نفسك بتهويسات البطالين، واقتد بأولى العزم والنهي من الانبياء
والصالحين، ولا تطمع في أن تحصد ما لم تزرع، وليت من صام وصلى وجاهد واتقى
غفر له.
فهذه جمل مما ينبغي أن تحفظ عنه جوارحك الظاهرة، وأعمال هذه الجوارح إنما
تترشح من صفات القلب؛ فإن أردت حفظ الجوارح فعليك بتطهير القلب؛ فهو تقوى
الباطن، والقلب هو المضغة التي إذا صلحت صلح الجسد بها سائر الجسد، وإذا
فسدت فسد بها سائر الجسد، فاشتغل باصلاحه لتصلح به جوارحك، وصلاحه يكون
بملازمة المراقبة.

### | القول في معاصى القلب

اعلم أن الصفات المذمومة في القلب كثيرة، وطريق تطهير القلب من رذائلها
طويلة، وسبيل العلاج فيها غامض، وقد اندرس بالكلية علمه وعمله؛ لغفلة الخلق
عن أنفسهم واشتغالهم بزخارف الدنيا.
وقد استقصينا ذلك كله في كتاب (إحياء علوم الدين) في ربع المهلكات وربع
المنجيات، ولكنا نحذرك؛ فإنها مهلكات في أنفسها، وهي أمهات لجملة من
الخبائب سواها: وهي

- Root: ق-د-م (Q-D-M) / ر-ج-ل (R-J-L)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Rijl" denotes the foot as an instrument of locomotion; "Qadam" implies precedence and forward movement toward a goal.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, the feet symbolize the physical means by which one pursues either obedience or transgression; movement is never morally neutral.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) walking is extended metaphorically (majāz) to "striving" (saʿy) toward a destination—whether righteous or corrupt.
- Root: ح-س-د (Ḥ-S-D)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Ḥasad" is the wish for the removal of another's blessing; rooted in the sense of "rubbing" or "wearing away."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A vice of the heart that opposes divine distributive justice (ʿadl); it is a rejection of God's allotment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal "wearing down" becomes metaphorical for the soul's corrosion through envy.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Protasis (Sharṭ) with Jazā' — The sentence "If you fall short (in striving), its evil consequence is upon you" employs a conditional construction where the apodosis is a nominal sentence, emphasizing the inescapable causal link between action and recompense.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the two feet—guard them from walking with them toward the forbidden, or hastening with them to the door of a tyrannical ruler. For walking to oppressive rulers, without necessity, is a grave sin and a burden of transgression; indeed, it is an act of self-abasement before them and an honoring of them for their injustice.

God—exalted is He—has commanded turning away from them in His saying: {«وَلَا تَرْكَنُوا إِلَى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا فَتَمَسَّكُمُ النَّارُ»} ("And do not incline toward those who have wronged, lest the Fire touch you"). This is an augmentation of their numbers; and if it is for the sake of seeking their wealth, then it is a striving toward the forbidden. The Prophet—peace be upon him—said: "Whoever humbles himself before a wealthy man for the sake of his wealth, two-thirds of his religion departs." This is said regarding a righteous wealthy man—so what do you think of a tyrannical wealthy man?

In sum, your movements and your stillness with your limbs are a grace from among the graces of God—exalted is He—upon you. So do not move any part of them in disobedience to God—exalted is He—at all; rather, employ them in obedience to God—exalted is He.

Know that if you fall short, its evil consequence is upon you; and if you exert yourself, its fruit returns to you. God is independent of you and of your deeds; rather, {«كُلُّ نَفْسٍ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ رَهِينَةٌ»} ("Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned").

Beware lest you say: "God is Generous and Merciful; He forgives sins for the disobedient." For this is a true word by which falsehood is intended. Its utterer is branded with foolishness (ḥamāqah), by the branding of the Messenger of God—peace be upon him—where he said: "The shrewd one is he who takes account of himself and works for what comes after death; and the foolish one is he who follows his soul's whims and harbors vain hopes upon God."

Know that this saying of yours is also the saying of one who wishes to become a jurist in the sciences of religion without studying any science, occupying himself with idleness, saying: "God is Generous and Merciful, capable of pouring upon my heart from the sciences what He poured upon the hearts of His prophets and saints, without effort, repetition, or learning." This is like the saying of one who desires wealth, yet abandons cultivation, trade, and earning, and remains idle, saying: "God is Generous and Merciful; to Him belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth; He is capable of revealing to me a treasure from among His treasures by which I am enriched without earning—for He has done this for some of His servants."

When you hear the speech of these two men, you deem them foolish and mock them—even though what they described of God's generosity and power is true and real. Likewise, the possessors of insight in religion laugh at you when you seek forgiveness without striving for it. God—exalted is He—says: {«وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ»} ("And that man has nothing but what he strives for"), and He says: {«إِنَّمَا تُجْزَوْنَ مَا كُنتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ»} ("You are only recompensed for what you used to do"), and He says: {«إِنَّ الْأَبْرَارَ لَفِي نَعِيمٍ وَإِنَّ الْفُجَّارَ لَفِي جَحِيمٍ»} ("Indeed, the righteous are in bliss, and indeed, the wicked are in Hellfire").

So if you do not abandon striving in seeking knowledge and wealth, relying upon His generosity, then likewise do not abandon provisioning for the Hereafter, and do not slacken. For the Lord of this world and the Hereafter is One; He is in both Generous and Merciful. His generosity is not increased by your obedience; rather, His generosity—glorified and exalted is He—lies in His facilitating for you the path to the abiding dominion and the perpetual, everlasting bliss, through patience in forsaking lusts for a few brief days. And this is the utmost limit of generosity.

So do not whisper to yourself the delusions of the idle. Follow the resolute and forbearing ones among the prophets and the righteous. Do not covet reaping what you have not sown. Would that the one who fasts, prays, strives, and is God-fearing be forgiven.

This is a summary of what your outward limbs ought to be guarded from. Yet the deeds of these limbs only emanate from the attributes of the heart. If you wish to guard the limbs, then you must purify the heart—for that is the inward piety (taqwā al-bāṭin). The heart is that lump of flesh (muḍghah) which, when sound, the whole body is sound through it; and when corrupt, the whole body is corrupt through it. So occupy yourself with its rectification, that your limbs may be rectified through it. And its rectification lies in the constant observance of watchfulness (murāqabah).

### | Discourse on the Sins of the Heart

Know that the blameworthy attributes of the heart are many; the path of purifying the heart from their vices is long; and the way of treating them is obscure. Its knowledge and practice have become entirely effaced, due to creation's heedlessness of their own souls and their occupation with the embellishments of this world.

We have exhaustively treated all of this in the book Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn, in the Quarter of the Destroyers (Rubʿ al-Muhlikāt) and the Quarter of the Saviors (Rubʿ al-Munjiyāt). But here we warn you—for they are destructive in themselves, and they are the mothers of a host of other corruptions besides them. They are:

### | Envy (ḥasad)

### | Ostentation (riyāʾ)

### | Self-Admiration (ʿujb)

So exert yourself in purifying your heart of them. If you are able to do so, then learn the manner of guarding against the rest of them from the Quarter of the Destroyers. But if you are incapable of this, then you are even more incapable of other things.

And do not suppose that you will be saved by a sound intention in learning knowledge while there remains in your heart anything of envy—

chapters.title_en: Section 19 — On the Vices of the Heart: Ostentation, Envy, Self-Admiration, and Pride
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الرياء

والعجب، وقد قال صلى الله عليه  وسلم: (ثلاث مهلكات: شح مطاع، وهوى متبع،
وإعجاب المرء بنفسه) .
الحسد
أما الحسد: فهو متشعب من الشح، فإن البخيل هو الذي يبخل بما في يده على
غيره، والشحيح هوالذي يبخل بنعمة الله تعالى وهي في خزائن قدرته تعالى، لا
في خزائنه، على عباد الله فشحه أعظم، والمحسود هو الذي يشق عليه إنعام الله
تعالى من خزائن قدرته، على عبد من عباده بعلم أو مال أو محبة في قلوب
الناس، أو حظ من الحظوظ، حتى أنه ليحب زوالها عنه، وإن لم يحصل له بذلك شيء
من تلك النعمة؛ فهذا منتهى الخبث؛ فلذلك قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:
(الحسد يأكل الحسنات كما تأكل النارالحطب) .
والحسود هو المعذب الذي لا يرحم، ولا يزال في عذاب دائم في الدنيا إلى
موته، ولعذاب الآخرة أشد وأكبر.
بل لا يصل العبد إلى حقيقة الإيمان ما لم يحب لسائر الناس ما يحب لنفسه،
بل ينبغي ان يساهم المسلمين في السراء والضراء؛ فالمسلمون كالبنيان الواحد
يشد بعضه بعضا، وكالجسد الواحد إذا اشتكى منه عضو اشتكى سائر الجسد. فإن
كنت لا تصادف هذا من قلبك، فاشتغالك بطلب التخلص من الهلاك أهم من اشتغالك
بنوادر الفروع وعلم الخصومات.
الرياء؟؟؟؟؟؟
وأما الرياء: فهو الشرك الخفي، وهو أحد الشركين، وذلك طلب المنزلة في
قلوب الخلق، لتنال بها الجاه والحشمة، وحب الجاه من الهوى المتبع، وفيه هلك
أكثر الناس، فما أهلك الناس إلا الناس، ولو أنصف الناس حقيقة لعلموا أن
أكثر ما هم فيه من العلوم والعبادات فضلا عن أعمال العادات، ليس يحملهم
يحملهم عليه إلا مراءاة الناس، وهي محبطة للأعمال، كما ورد الخبر: (أن
الشهيد يؤمر به يوم القيامة إلى النار، فيقول: يا رب استشهدت في سبيلك،
فيقول الله تعالى: بل أردت أن يقال إنك شجاع، وقد قيل ذلك،
وذلك أجرك - وكذلك يقال للعالم والحاج والقارىء.

### | العجب والكبر والفخر

وأما العجب والكبر والفخر: فهو الداء العضال، وهو نظر العبد إلى نفسه
بعين العز والاستظام، وإلى غيره بعين الاحتقار والذل، ونتيجته على  اللسان
أن يقول: أنا وأنا كما قال إبليس اللعين: (أنا خير منه، خلقتني من نار،
وخلقته من طين) وثمرته في المجالس الترفع والتقدم وطلب التصدر فيها، وفي
المحاورة الاستنكاف من أن يرد كلامه عليه.
والمتكبرهو الذي إن وعظ أنف، أو وعظ عنف، فكل من رأى نفسه خيرا من أحد من
خلق الله تعالى فهو متكبر.
بل ينبغي لك أن تعلم أن الخير من هو خير عند الله في دار الآخرة، وذلك
غيب، وهو موقوف على الخاتمة؛ فاعتقادك في نفسك أنك خير من غيرك جهل محض، بل
ينبغي ألا تنظر إلى أحد إلا وترى أنه خير منك، وأن الفضل له على نفسك، فإن
رأيت صغيرا قلت: هذا لم يعص الله وأنا عصيته، فلا شك أنه خير مني وإن رأيت
كبيرا قلت هذا قد عبد الله قبلى، فلا شك أنه خير مني وإن رأيت كبيرا قلت
هذا قد عبد الله قبلي، فلا شك أنه خير مني وإن رأيت كبيرا قلت هذا قد عبد
الله قبلي، فلا شك أنه خير مني. وإن كان عالما قلت: هذا قد أعطى ما لم أعط،
وبلغ ما لم أبلغ، وعلم ما جهلت؛ فكيف أكون مثله وإن كان جاهلا قلت: هذا قد
عصى الله بجهل، وأنا عصيته بعلم؛ فحجة الله على آكد، وما أدري بم يختم لي
وبم يختم له؟ وإن كان كافرا قلت: لا أدري، عسى أن يسلم ويختم له بخير
العمل، وينسل بإسلامه من الذنوب كما تنسل الشعرة من العجين، وأما أنا -
والعياذ بالله - فعسى أن يضلني الله فأكفر فيختم لي بشر العمل؛ فيكون غدا
هو من المقربين، وأنا أكون من المبعدين.
فلا يخرج الكبر من قلبك إلا بأن تعرف أن الكبير من هو كبير عند الله
تعالى، وذلك موقوف على الخاتمة، وهي مشكوك فيه؛ فيشغلك خوف الخاتمة عن أن
تتكبر مع الشك فيها على عباد الله تعالى، فيقينك وإيمانك في الحال لا يناقض
تجويزك في الاستقبال؛ فإن الله مقلب القلوب يهدي من يشاء، ويضل من  يشاء.

### | حديث جامع في معاصي القلب
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ي-أ (r-y-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To show, to display; riyāʾ is the act of exhibiting deeds for the sake of being seen by others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The seeking of status (manzilah) in the hearts of creatures, a form of hidden shirk (associationism) that nullifies devotional acts.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is visual perception; metaphorically, it denotes the inward orientation of intention toward created beholders rather than the Creator.
- Root: ح-س-د (ḥ-s-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To wish for the removal of a blessing from another; the root also conveys the notion of "wearing away" or "corroding."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A moral disease stemming from avarice (shuḥḥ); it opposes the Quranic ideal of preferring others over oneself (īthār).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: the erosion of something; metaphorical: the consuming of good deeds by envy, as fire consumes wood.
- Root: ع-ج-ب (ʿ-j-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Astonishment; ʿujb is self-amazement, a state where one deems his own deeds superior without recognizing divine grace.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A hidden form of pride (kibr) rooted in ignorance of one's own defects and of God's sovereignty over outcomes.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: wonder; metaphorical: the heart's complacency with its own virtue, which blinds it to the precariousness of the final end (khātimah).
- Root: ك-ب-ر (k-b-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Bigness, greatness; takabbur is the assumption of superiority over others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The disposition of viewing oneself with the eye of exaltation and others with the eye of contempt; its archetype is Iblīs's refusal to prostrate.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical magnitude; metaphorical: moral arrogance, which is forbidden because true greatness belongs solely to God.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Clauses (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The repeated conditional structures (e.g., "If you see a child... say...") require the apodosis to be a command or statement of obligation, as employed here to prescribe a fixed ethical response in each hypothetical scenario.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the vices of the heart are many, but the most destructive among them are ostentation (riyāʾ), self-admiration (ʿujb), envy (ḥasad), and pride (kibr). The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Three things are destructive: avarice obeyed, passion followed, and a man's self-admiration of his own soul.»

As for envy (ḥasad): it branches forth from avarice (shuḥḥ). For the miser (bakhīl) is one who withholds what is in his own hand from others, whereas the avaricious one (shaḥīḥ) is he who withholds the blessings of God Almighty — which lie in the treasuries of His power, not in his own treasuries — from the servants of God. Thus his avarice is greater. The envier (ḥāsid) is one who finds it grievous that God Almighty should bestow, from the treasuries of His power, a blessing upon one of His servants — whether it be knowledge, wealth, love in the hearts of people, or any share of worldly fortune — to the point that he desires its removal from that person, even if he himself gains nothing of that blessing by its removal. This is the extreme of malice. Therefore, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Envy consumes good deeds just as fire consumes wood.»

The envier is the tormented one who is shown no mercy; he remains in perpetual torment in this world until his death, and the torment of the Hereafter is more severe and greater.

Indeed, a servant does not attain the reality of faith (ḥaqīqat al-īmān) until he loves for all people what he loves for himself. Rather, he ought to share with the Muslims in their prosperity and adversity; for the Muslims are like a single edifice, parts of which strengthen other parts, and like a single body — when one member complains, the rest of the body shares in the fever and sleeplessness. If you do not find this disposition in your heart, then your occupation with seeking deliverance from perdition is more important than your occupation with the rare branches of jurisprudence and the science of disputations.

As for ostentation (riyāʾ): it is the hidden shirk (al-shirk al-khafī), and it is one of the two forms of shirk. It consists in seeking a station in the hearts of creatures, so that one may attain thereby prestige and reverence. The love of prestige (ḥubb al-jāh) is part of the passion that is followed, and through it most people are destroyed. For nothing destroys people except people themselves. Were people to be truly fair, they would know that most of what they engage in — of sciences and acts of worship, let alone customary deeds — is driven by nothing but showing off to people. And this nullifies deeds, as the report has come: «The martyr will be commanded on the Day of Resurrection toward the Fire, and he will say: "O Lord, I was martyred in Your path." God Almighty will say: "Rather, you intended that it be said that you are brave, and it was said — and that is your reward."» And likewise it will be said to the scholar, the pilgrim, and the reciter of the Quran.

As for self-admiration (ʿujb), pride (kibr), and vainglory (fakhr): they constitute the chronic disease (al-dāʾ al-ʿuḍāl). It is the servant's looking at himself with the eye of exaltation and self-magnification, and at others with the eye of contempt and belittlement. Its outcome upon the tongue is that he says "I, I" — just as Iblīs, the accursed, said: «I am better than him; You created me from fire, and You created him from clay.» Its fruit in gatherings is self-elevation, precedence, and seeking the seat of honor; and in conversation, it is the disdain of having one's speech returned upon him.

The arrogant one (mutakabbir) is he who, if admonished, takes offense, or if he admonishes, does so harshly. So whoever sees himself as better than any of God's creatures is arrogant.

Rather, you ought to know that the good person is he who is good in the sight of God in the abode of the Hereafter — and that is unseen (ghayb), dependent upon the final end (khātimah). Thus, your belief in yourself that you are better than another is pure ignorance. Rather, you should not look at anyone except that you see him as better than yourself, and that he has precedence over you. If you see a child, you say: "This one has not disobeyed God, whereas I have disobeyed Him — so there is no doubt that he is better than me." If you see an elder, you say: "This one has worshipped God before me — so there is no doubt that he is better than me." If you see a scholar, you say: "This one has been given what I have not been given, has reached what I have not reached, and knows what I have been ignorant of — so how could I be his equal?" If you see an ignorant person, you say: "This one has disobeyed God out of ignorance, whereas I have disobeyed Him with knowledge — so the proof of God against me is more conclusive. And I do not know with what end it will be sealed for me, nor with what end it will be sealed for him." If you see a disbeliever, you say: "I do not know — perhaps he will embrace Islam and be sealed with the best of deeds, and his sins will fall away through his Islam as a hair falls away from dough. As for me — God forbid — perhaps God will lead me astray so that I disbelieve and am sealed with the worst of deeds. Thus tomorrow he will be among those brought near, and I will be among those cast far."

Pride will not depart from your heart until you know that the great one is he who is great in the sight of God Almighty — and that is dependent upon the final end, which is a matter of doubt. Thus, the fear of the final end will occupy you from being arrogant, in a state of doubt, toward the servants of God Almighty. For your certainty and faith in the present moment does not contradict your allowance of possibility in the future; indeed, God is the Turner of Hearts (muqallib al-qulūb); He guides whom He wills and leads astray whom He wills.

chapters.title_en: The Vices of the Heart: Envy, Pride, Ostentation, and Self-Admiration — A Hadith on the Veils That Block Works from Allah
